It is useful when several current attribute values are needed at once rather than retrieving each individually. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/attributes.md

GetAttributeChangedSignal is an Instance method that returns a ScriptSignal firing whenever the specified attribute changes. Its signature is `Instance:GetAttributeChangedSignal(Attribute: string)` and the parameter is the name of the attribute to watch. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, this signal can be obtained but its callback delivery has not been confirmed, so polling is recommended instead. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/attributes.md

questions: What is Vortex Studio 0.3.4 Attribute Compatibility?
Explain Vortex Studio 0.3.4 Attribute Compatibility in Vortex
How do I use Vortex Studio 0.3.4 Attribute Compatibility?
Tell me about Vortex Studio 0.3.4 Attribute Compatibility
answer: In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, attribute methods are confirmed to work on Part instances, while Player instances are not attribute-capable and all attribute methods return nil on them. Server-to-client and client-to-server Character attribute replication are both confirmed through the current player's Character Model, so a LocalScript can observe server-set Character attributes and a server Script can observe client-set ones. Attribute values written by clients should not be trusted as authoritative input since the server accepts what the client sends. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/attributes.md

BindableEvent is a type that can be created in Vortex Studio. It exposes an `Event` table that is accessible from both Script and LocalScript contexts. However, the `BindableEvent:Fire(...)` method needed to actually fire the event is not available in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/bindable-events.md

`BindableEvent:Fire(...)` is the method that would normally be used to emit or trigger a BindableEvent. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, this method is unavailable, so events cannot actually be invoked through it on that version. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/bindable-events.md

questions: What is script-to-script messaging with BindableEvent?
Explain BindableEvent script-to-script messaging in Vortex
How do I send messages between scripts using BindableEvent?
Tell me about BindableEvent script-to-script messaging
answer: Because `BindableEvent:Fire(...)` is missing in Vortex Studio 0.3.4, BindableEvents cannot currently be used to pass messages between scripts. Developers are advised to use a shared state mechanism instead, or an authored RemoteEvent when the communication needs to cross client/server boundaries. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/bindable-events.md

questions: What is the client-server model in Vortex?
Explain the client-server model in Vortex
How do I use the client-server model?
Tell me about the client-server model
answer: Vortex games run on a client-server architecture where the server acts as the authoritative source of game state and clients are local copies running on each player's device. The server manages trusted data such as player data, damage, money, and game rules, while the client handles visuals, UI, animations, and input. Server code runs in Scripts, and client code runs in LocalScripts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/client-server.md

questions: What is the Server in Vortex?
How do I use the Server?
answer: The Server is the authoritative side of a Vortex game. It runs separately from the player's device and is responsible for managing the actual state of the game, including player data, game rules, damage, and money. Server-side code is executed from Script instances, which the server runs to keep trusted state synchronized between players. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/client-server.md

questions: What is the Client in Vortex?
How do I use the Client?
answer: The Client is the player's side of a Vortex game. It runs on the player's local device and handles what the player directly sees and interacts with, such as rendering the world, displaying UI, playing animations, and receiving input. Client-side code is executed from LocalScript instances. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/client-server.md

questions: What is Client to Server remote validation in Vortex?
Explain Client to Server remote validation in Vortex
How do I use Client to Server remote validation?
Tell me about Client to Server remote validation
answer: When handling client-to-server remote communication, the server must validate any data sent by the client because the client cannot be trusted to make authoritative decisions. The recommended pattern is to let the client signal intent only, while the server performs the actual state changes. For example, a buy button should send a purchase request to the server, which then checks if the player has enough money and grants the item, rather than the client modifying its own money and inventory before notifying the server. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/client-server.md

questions: What are the Studio 0.3.4 remote sender limitations in Vortex?
Explain the Studio 0.3.4 remote sender limitations in Vortex
How do I work with the Studio 0.3.4 remote sender limitations?
Tell me about the Studio 0.3.4 remote sender limitations
answer: In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, client-to-server is the only confirmed remote direction, and the server receives a numeric connection identifier rather than a Player object from the sender. A server Script can call Players:GetPlayers() to enumerate active players and access their Characters, but there is no public way to map the sender id back to a specific Player. As a result, server logic can validate and process a request, but it cannot reliably use the typical Roblox pattern of targeting the calling player's Character. Additionally, server visibility is not equivalent to authority, so writing a Humanoid's Health property on the visible character from a server Script is still rejected. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/client-server.md

In Vortex, a Signal is a runtime event representation used to broadcast and consume notifications. Signals can be connected with the `:Connect` method, which accepts a callback function and returns a Connection that should be held onto. The `:Once` and `:Wait` helpers are also exposed, while `:ConnectParallel` is intentionally not available. When manually triggering an event with `:Fire(...)`, delivery works reliably for standalone and supported signals. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

Signal:Connect attaches a listener callback to a signal so it runs every time the signal fires. It returns a Connection object that the caller must store in order to manage the subscription. The callback receives whatever values the producer passes to `:Fire(...)`, such as deltaTime from RunService.Heartbeat. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

Signal:Once is an available variant of connection that fires the listener only a single time, after which it automatically disconnects. It is useful for one-shot handlers where retaining and manually disconnecting a Connection would be unnecessary. It is exposed alongside Connect and Wait on supported signal types. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

Signal:Wait yields the current coroutine until the signal fires, then returns the arguments passed to `:Fire(...)`. It is the preferred way to pause execution at a synchronization point without writing a manual Connect/Disconnect pair. Wait is exposed as part of the supported signal API. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

Signal:Fire manually triggers delivery of the signal and forwards its arguments to every connected listener. Manual firing is fully supported on standalone signals and on signals Vortex explicitly implements, while a small set of instance change signals are connectable but do not actually fire when their backing property or attribute is written. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

A Connection is the object returned by Signal:Connect (and similar methods) that represents an active subscription to a signal. It exists so listeners can later detach their callback via `:Disconnect`. Holding the reference is the standard way to manage signal lifetime in Vortex code. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

Connection:Disconnect removes the listener associated with that Connection from its Signal, stopping future deliveries. It is the cleanup step that pairs with Signal:Connect once the listener is no longer needed. Calling Disconnect more than once is safe, since the connection is no longer subscribed after the first call. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

questions: Explain Event delivery limitations in Vortex
How do I use Event delivery limitations?
Tell me about Event delivery limitations
answer: Vortex does not implement every Roblox-style event uniformly: manual Signal:Fire(...) delivery works for standalone and supported signals, but some instance change signals can be connected yet never fire when their underlying property or attribute is written. Specific cases like Part.Changed, user input, Humanoid health signals, and RemoteEvent signals must be handled according to their individually documented runtime behavior rather than assumed to be live. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

questions: What is the rule about Connectable signals as producer proof?
Explain Connectable signals as producer proof in Vortex
How do I use Connectable signals as producer proof?
Tell me about Connectable signals as producer proof
answer: In Vortex, being able to call :Connect on a signal does not prove that anything will ever fire it, since some instance change signals are wired up for connection only and do not actually dispatch. The documented guidance is to verify that the specific event delivers in the context where your code runs before relying on it as a real-time producer. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/events.md

questions: What is Hello World Script in Vortex?
Explain Hello World Script in Vortex
How do I use Hello World Script in Vortex?
Tell me about Hello World Script in Vortex
answer: The Hello World script is the introductory script in Vortex, placed inside ServerScriptService. When the game is playtested, running this script causes the text 'Hello, world!' to appear in the output window. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/first-script.md

questions: What is Spawning a Part in Workspace?
Explain Spawning a Part in Workspace in Vortex
How do I use Spawning a Part in Workspace in Vortex?
Tell me about Spawning a Part in Workspace
answer: Spawning a part in Workspace is a common introductory technique in Vortex where a script obtains the Workspace service using game:GetService("Workspace"), creates a new Part via Instance.new("Part"), and assigns the created part as a child of Workspace by setting part.Parent = workspace. Once parented, the part becomes visible in the game world during playtesting. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/first-script.md

questions: Explain Configuring Part Properties in Vortex
How do I use Configuring Part Properties in Vortex?
Tell me about Configuring Part Properties
answer: After creating a part, its appearance and behavior can be customized by assigning values to its properties. In Vortex you can set part.Name = "MyPart", part.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2), part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0), part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(192, 32, 12), and part.Anchored = false. Anchoring a part false allows physics to act on it, while setting position, size, name, and color control its location, scale, identifier, and visual appearance. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/first-script.md

An Instance is the fundamental building block for every object in a Vortex game, similar to Roblox's Instance model. There are many types of Instances, and each one has its own set of Properties along with unique behaviors. Instances form the basis of the entire game object hierarchy in Vortex Studio. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/instances.md

Instance.new is a global method used to create a new Instance in a script. It takes the ClassName of the desired Instance type as its first argument. This is the primary way developers instantiate objects programmatically in Vortex. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/instances.md

Vortex is a game development platform inspired by Roblox that enables creators to build projects ranging from simple games to large, complex experiences using the Luau scripting language. It provides a development environment for designing game worlds and the logic that drives them. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/intro.md

questions: How do I use Vortex Engine?
answer: Vortex Engine is the API layer provided by the Vortex platform. It exposes functionality for constructing games, spawning parts, writing scripts, responding to events, and other core development tasks. The scripting documentation describes how to use this engine within your projects. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/intro.md

questions: What is Your First Script guide?
Explain Your First Script guide in Vortex
How do I use Your First Script guide?
Tell me about Your First Script guide
answer: Your First Script is a beginner guide intended for new users of Vortex Studio. It walks through creating an initial script and serves as the recommended starting point before exploring the broader scripting API. It is referenced from the documentation's introduction page. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/intro.md

In Vortex, instance properties are accessed using dot syntax for reading and assignment for writing. The set of properties an instance exposes depends on its class, and certain runtime authority rules apply to character state. Temporary Parts in Vortex Studio 0.3.4 allow writable access to appearance, transform, collision, anchoring, and name properties, while live character properties such as Humanoid health and root-part transform cannot be written even from a server Script. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/properties.md

questions: What is Reading optional properties safely?
Explain Reading optional properties safely in Vortex
How do I use Reading optional properties safely?
Tell me about Reading optional properties safely
answer: When a property may not be accessible, Vortex commonly returns nil on the read instead of raising an error. To distinguish between an unavailable member and a failed read, wrap the access in pcall. A typical pattern captures both the success flag and the returned value, then checks that the call succeeded and the value is not nil before using it. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/properties.md

questions: How do I use Change signals?
answer: Changed, GetPropertyChangedSignal, and attribute-change signals may exist and be connectable on an instance but still fail to fire after a property is written. For situations where correctness requires observing an actual change, the recommended approach is to poll the property rather than rely on signal delivery. Further details are available in the Signals and Attributes documentation pages. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/properties.md

A RemoteEvent is a one-way communication object used to send messages between the server and clients in Vortex. Unlike RemoteFunctions, it does not wait for a response and produces no return value, making it suitable for notifying the other side that something happened rather than requesting a result. RemoteEvents are typically parented under ReplicatedStorage so that both server scripts and client scripts can access them. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

FireServer is a method on RemoteEvent that is called from a client to send arguments to the server. It returns void and triggers the OnServerEvent handler on the server. The page warns that arguments from clients must never be trusted without re-validation on the server, since a modified client could send anything. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

FireClient is a method on RemoteEvent called from the server to send arguments to a specific chosen client. It returns void. As of Vortex Studio 0.3.4, this method is exposed but its delivery is noted as unconfirmed. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

FireAllClients is a method on RemoteEvent called from the server to broadcast arguments to every connected client. It returns void. According to the Vortex Studio 0.3.4 notes, this method is exposed but its delivery behavior is unconfirmed. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

OnServerEvent is an event on RemoteEvent that fires on the server when a client invokes FireServer. Its first parameter is described in the 0.3.4 notes as a numeric connection id rather than a Player instance, so the server must use GetPlayers() to look up player information. It also accepts any additional arguments forwarded from the client's FireServer call. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

OnClientEvent is an event on RemoteEvent that fires on the client when the server invokes FireClient or FireAllClients. It accepts the arguments forwarded from the server call. As of Vortex Studio 0.3.4, this event is exposed but its delivery remains unconfirmed. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

questions: How do I secure RemoteEvent calls?
Tell me about RemoteEvent security considerations
answer: RemoteEvents are inherently insecure because a modified client can call FireServer with arbitrary arguments. Any data received from a client via OnServerEvent should be re-validated on the server before being acted upon, and the page explicitly warns against trusting client arguments at face value. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

questions: What is the RemoteEvent placement guideline in ReplicatedStorage?
How do I place RemoteEvents in ReplicatedStorage?
Tell me about RemoteEvent in ReplicatedStorage
answer: ReplicatedStorage is the recommended parent container for RemoteEvents because it is visible and accessible to both server scripts and client scripts. The 0.3.4 notes add that editor-authored remotes in ReplicatedStorage correctly dispatch from FireServer to OnServerEvent, while script-created remotes were visible to clients but did not dispatch in the tested runtime. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

questions: Explain RemoteEvent argument restrictions in Vortex
How do I pass arguments to RemoteEvent?
Tell me about RemoteEvent argument limitations
answer: As of Vortex Studio 0.3.4, RemoteEvent arguments cannot contain Instances, which means objects like LocalPlayer or a Character cannot be passed through FireServer or FireClient. Servers and clients must instead pass primitive data such as numbers, strings, booleans, or Color3 values. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

questions: What is the ChangeColor RemoteEvent example?
Explain the ChangeColor example in Vortex
How do I build a color-changing RemoteEvent?
Tell me about the ChangeColor example
answer: The ChangeColor example demonstrates a RemoteEvent that changes a part named ColorBlock to a random color when a player presses E. A LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts listens for the E key via UserInputService.InputBegan and calls changeColor:FireServer() with no arguments, while a server script in ServerScriptService connects to changeColor.OnServerEvent and sets colorBlock.Color to a random Color3.fromRGB value. This pattern is needed because key presses can only be observed on the client but the color change must occur on the server so every player sees the same result. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-events.md

RemoteFunction is a class that allows two-way remote invocation between client and server in Vortex. An editor-authored RemoteFunction placed in ReplicatedStorage exposes InvokeServer to LocalScripts, and a server Script can assign a function to OnServerInvoke to handle incoming requests. However, RemoteFunctions are currently limited in Vortex Studio 0.3.4 and are not recommended for required gameplay paths. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-functions.md

InvokeServer is the client-side method on a RemoteFunction that a LocalScript uses to send a request to the server and wait for a response. It is exposed when a RemoteFunction is placed in ReplicatedStorage. Currently, passing instance arguments such as LocalPlayer to InvokeServer fails before delivery with an "Instances cannot be sent" runtime error, and a successful primitive request/response round trip has not yet been established in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-functions.md

OnServerInvoke is the callback property on a RemoteFunction that a server Script assigns to a function in order to process requests received from clients via InvokeServer. When invoked, the assigned function is expected to return a value that is sent back to the requesting client. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4 this round-trip path has not been confirmed as fully working with primitive payloads. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-functions.md

questions: What is the RemoteFunction instance argument limitation?
Explain RemoteFunction instance argument limitation in Vortex
How do I handle RemoteFunction instance argument limitation?
Tell me about RemoteFunction instance argument limitation
answer: RemoteFunction calls in Vortex do not support instance arguments. If a client invokes a RemoteFunction while passing a Roblox-style Instance such as LocalPlayer, the call fails before it reaches the server with a runtime error reading "Instances cannot be sent". Only primitive values can be passed as arguments, and even then the full primitive round trip is not yet confirmed in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-functions.md

questions: How do I use RemoteEvent as an alternative?
answer: When one-way client-to-server communication is sufficient, Vortex developers are advised to use an editor-authored RemoteEvent in ReplicatedStorage with primitive payloads instead of a RemoteFunction. RemoteEvent delivery has been observed working in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. One quirk is that the server-sender value on a received RemoteEvent is exposed as a numeric identifier rather than a full Player object. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/remote-functions.md

topic: Script and LocalScript Globals in Vortex Studio 0.3.4
questions: What is the globals restriction for Script and LocalScript in Vortex?
How do I use Script globals in Vortex?
Tell me about Script globals in Vortex
answer: In Vortex Studio version 0.3.4, both Script and LocalScript instances lack a number of standard Lua globals. These include `require`, `load`, `loadstring`, `loadfile`, `dofile`, `io`, `os`, `package`, `debug`, `bit32`, `buffer`, `vector`, and `shared`. As a result, scripts cannot dynamically load code, interact with the operating system, or manipulate buffers and vectors directly. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

questions: What filesystem and hook globals are unavailable in Vortex?
How do I use filesystem globals in Vortex?
Tell me about hook globals in Vortex
answer: Executor-style helpers for reading, writing, listing, or deleting files are not exposed in Vortex Studio. Globals such as `readfile`, `writefile`, `appendfile`, `listfiles`, `isfile`, `isfolder`, `makefolder`, `delfile`, `getgenv`, `getrenv`, `getgc`, and `hookfunction` all evaluate to `nil`, so any attempt to call them will error. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

questions: What game entry points are restricted in Vortex?
Explain privileged game globals in Vortex
How do I use game entry points in Vortex?
Tell me about game entry points in Vortex
answer: Several methods on the `game` object that would normally grant elevated capabilities are blocked. Specifically, `game.HttpGet`, `game.HttpPost`, `game.GetObjects`, `game.Loaded`, and `Instance.fromExisting` are unavailable, preventing external HTTP requests, asset insertion, and construction of instances from external sources. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

questions: What services are not available in Vortex?
Explain blocked Roblox services in Vortex
How do I use services in Vortex?
Tell me about unavailable services in Vortex
answer: Common Roblox services that interact with the network, persistence, or marketplace are not valid services in either the server or client execution context. These include `HttpService`, `DataStoreService`, `TeleportService`, `MarketplaceService`, and `InsertService`, all of which cannot be obtained via `game:GetService`. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

questions: What reflection helpers are exposed in Vortex?
Explain Lua reflection helpers in Vortex
How do I use reflection helpers in Vortex?
Tell me about reflection helpers in Vortex
answer: Vortex Studio exposes a set of standard Lua reflection helpers that operate on tables, metatables, and proxies. These are `getfenv`, `setfenv`, `getmetatable`, `setmetatable`, `rawget`, `rawset`, `rawequal`, `newproxy`, `collectgarbage`, and the global `_G` table. Their availability does not grant scripts any path to escape the sandbox. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

questions: What isolation does the sandbox provide in Vortex?
How do I use the sandbox in Vortex?
Tell me about sandbox isolation in Vortex
answer: Scripts in Vortex Studio are treated as isolated from the host filesystem, from arbitrary code loading, from external networking, and from privileged Roblox services. The combination of removed globals, blocked game methods, and missing services enforces these boundaries, and reflection helpers like `_G` or `getfenv` do not provide a workaround. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/sandbox-limits.md

A Script is a container object that holds Luau source code and is used to define gameplay logic and interact with the Vortex engine. Its source code is not executed directly by the container itself; instead, the engine passes the source to the Luau runtime where the Luau VM compiles and runs it. Scripts can implement complex gameplay systems beyond simple tasks like creating instances, and the two currently supported script types are LocalScript and Script. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/scripts-and-vms.md

LocalScript is one of the two script container types currently supported in Vortex. Like the Script type, it holds Luau source code that is compiled and executed by the Luau VM, but it is intended for client-side execution contexts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/scripts-and-vms.md

questions: What is the Luau Virtual Machine?
Explain the Luau Virtual Machine in Vortex
How do I use the Luau Virtual Machine?
Tell me about the Luau Virtual Machine
answer: The Luau Virtual Machine (VM) is the runtime component that executes compiled Luau bytecode. When a script runs, the engine retrieves its source code, the Luau compiler converts it into bytecode, and the Luau VM then carries out execution. The VM manages execution state including values, function calls, control flow, and other runtime operations. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/scripts-and-vms.md

questions: Explain the execution pipeline in Vortex
How do I use the execution pipeline?
Tell me about the execution pipeline
answer: The execution pipeline in Vortex describes how Luau code travels from storage to running on the game: Script stores the source code, the Luau compiler converts that source code into bytecode, the Luau VM executes the resulting bytecode, and engine APIs provide the functionality needed for that code to interact with the game and engine systems. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/scripts-and-vms.md

questions: How do I use Vortex engine integration?
Tell me about Vortex engine integration
answer: Vortex is built on top of Bevy, which serves as its underlying engine layer. Engine functionality is exposed to Luau through Vortex's scripting APIs, which allow scripts to interact with game objects and engine systems at runtime. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/scripts-and-vms.md

questions: How do I use Studio Keybindings?
answer: Studio Keybindings is a reference for the keyboard shortcuts and mouse controls available in Vortex Studio's editor. It covers shortcuts grouped into categories such as File, Editing, Text, Tools, Camera, Selection, and Window. These bindings let users save, undo, copy, paste, group, transform, navigate the viewport, select objects, and adjust the UI. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use File Shortcuts?
answer: The File shortcut category in Vortex Studio includes pressing Ctrl + S to save the current work. It is the only shortcut listed under the File section of the editor's keybinding reference. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Editing Shortcuts?
answer: Editing shortcuts in Vortex Studio provide quick access to common manipulation commands. Ctrl + Z undoes, Ctrl + C copies the selection, and Ctrl + V pastes copied parts. Ctrl + D duplicates selected nodes or parts, Ctrl + G groups selected parts into a model, and Shift + Ctrl + G ungroups a model. F focuses the view on the selected parts, and Backspace or Delete removes the selected parts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Text Shortcuts?
answer: Text shortcuts in Vortex Studio mirror standard text editing controls. Ctrl + A selects all text, Ctrl + C copies, Ctrl + V pastes, and Ctrl + X cuts the highlighted text. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Tools Shortcuts?
answer: Tool shortcuts in Vortex Studio let users switch modes by pressing number keys. Press 1 for Select mode, 2 for Move mode, 3 for Rotate mode, and 4 for Scale mode. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Camera Shortcuts?
answer: Camera shortcuts in Vortex Studio allow navigation of the viewport using the keyboard and mouse. W, A, S, and D move the camera forward, left, backward, and right, with Shift slowing the movement. Q and E move the camera down and up respectively. The scroll wheel moves the camera toward or away from the cursor, middle mouse drag pans the view, and holding right-click while dragging moves the view. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Selection Shortcuts?
answer: Selection shortcuts in Vortex Studio control how items are chosen in the editor. Left-click selects an item, Ctrl + click toggles individual nodes, and Shift + click selects multiple in the viewport or all items between two points in the Explorer. Left-click and drag creates a selection area for parts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

questions: How do I use Window Shortcuts?
answer: Window shortcuts in Vortex Studio manage the editor's display. F11 toggles fullscreen mode, and Ctrl combined with the minus or plus key decreases or increases the Studio UI size. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/studio/keybindings.md

task.spawn is a scheduling helper available in both Script and LocalScript contexts in Vortex Studio. It takes a callback function and runs it immediately within the current scheduling call. In the tested runtime, a callback passed to task.spawn completes before the scheduler yields control back. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/tasks.md

task.defer is a scheduling helper available in Script and LocalScript that queues its callback to run on a later scheduler cycle rather than immediately. In the tested runtime, the deferred callback remained pending after the first task.wait() call and ran during the subsequent scheduler cycle. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/tasks.md

task.delay is a scheduling helper that takes a duration and a callback, running the callback after approximately the specified time has elapsed. When called with a duration of 0, it behaves like task.defer, remaining pending through the first scheduler cycle and running on the next one. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/tasks.md

task.wait is a scheduling helper that yields the current scheduler cycle and resumes on a later one, returning a numeric value representing elapsed time. It is available in both Script and LocalScript contexts and serves as the primary way to observe scheduler progression in Vortex. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/tasks.md

questions: Explain Task scheduling behavior in Vortex
How do I use Task scheduling behavior?
Tell me about Task scheduling behavior
answer: Vortex Studio 0.3.4 scheduling follows a discrete cycle model: callbacks passed to task.spawn complete within the current scheduling call, while callbacks queued via task.defer or task.delay(0, callback) remain pending through the first task.wait() and complete during the second scheduler cycle. The helpers task.cancel, task.desynchronize, and task.synchronize are not available in this version. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/tasks.md

IntValue is a detached instance container in Vortex that holds a numeric value. It starts at 0 and exposes a Value property that is readable and writable from both Script and LocalScript contexts. You create one with Instance.new("IntValue") and assign to its Value property. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

StringValue is a detached instance container in Vortex that holds a string value. It starts as an empty string ("") and exposes a Value property that is accessible from both Script and LocalScript. It is constructed via Instance.new("StringValue") and assigned through the Value property. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

BoolValue is not constructable in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. When you need instance-backed state, the recommended approach is to use a plain Lua boolean for local state or an IntValue with a 0/1 convention. There is no constructor exposed for BoolValue at this time. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

questions: How do I use value containers?
answer: Vortex Studio 0.3.4 supports two simple script-visible value containers: IntValue and StringValue. Both are detached instances created via Instance.new() with default starting values of 0 and "" respectively, and both expose a Value property that can be read and written from Script and LocalScript. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

questions: Explain the Changed signal in Vortex
How do I use the Changed signal?
Tell me about the Changed signal
answer: Value instances in Vortex expose a Changed signal, but in the tested runtime it did not fire after a Value assignment. As a result, relying on Changed for game logic is unreliable. Developers should read or poll the Value property directly instead of subscribing to this signal. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

GetPropertyChangedSignal("Value") is available on IntValue and StringValue instances, but in the tested Vortex runtime it did not deliver callbacks when Value was reassigned. The signal is therefore not dependable for reactive game logic. Polling the Value property is recommended instead. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/guides/values.md

BindableEvent in Vortex is a constructable instance representing a partially exposed local-event object. It became available in Vortex Studio version 0.3.4 and can be created in both Script and LocalScript contexts using Instance.new("BindableEvent"). The instance exposes an Event property which returns a signal table, but it does not expose a Fire method, meaning scripts are not able to manually trigger the signal. Because triggering is unavailable, its practical role as an in-process event bus is currently limited in the runtime. The instance still has a Destroy method for cleanup. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/bindable-event.md

Event is a property of the BindableEvent instance in Vortex that returns a signal table. This signal can be connected to in the usual way, but since BindableEvent lacks a Fire method, there is no way for scripts to emit the event. The returned signal table is the only exposed means of interacting with the event through BindableEvent. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/bindable-event.md

Fire is not implemented on BindableEvent in Vortex. Accessing instance.Fire yields nil, so scripts cannot trigger the BindableEvent's signal. This absence is what makes BindableEvent unsuitable as an in-process event bus in the current Vortex runtime. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/bindable-event.md

BoolValue is a Roblox-compatible boolean value container class that is not supported in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Calling Instance.new("BoolValue") fails with an unable-to-create-instance error in both Script and LocalScript contexts. As a workaround, developers should use a native Lua boolean value, or alternatively use an IntValue instance that follows a documented convention of representing false as 0 and true as 1. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/bool-value.md

In Vortex, a Character is the runtime Model instance associated with a Player, exposed through the Player.Character field. It is not a separately constructible class; you obtain it from Players.LocalPlayer in a LocalScript or from Players:GetPlayers() in a server Script. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4 it reports ClassName == "Model" and is a live, queryable projection rather than a full Instance with all APIs. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

questions: Explain Character public fields in Vortex
How do I use Character public fields?
Tell me about Character public fields
answer: The Character's confirmed public projection exposes the fields ClassName, Name, Position, Humanoid, and HumanoidRootPart. Parent reads as nil on the projection. Standard R6/R15 limb names are absent from this public surface, although FindFirstChild("Humanoid") and FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart") resolve the same values as the public fields. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

questions: What is Character generic Instance methods?
Explain Character generic Instance methods in Vortex
How do I use Character generic Instance methods?
Tell me about Character generic Instance methods
answer: The Character supports tested generic Instance methods including GetChildren, GetDescendants, FindFirstChild, FindFirstChildOfClass, WaitForChild, and IsA, plus attribute and property-signal methods. Its hierarchy and lifecycle signals are unavailable, but the Changed signal is connectable. Model pivot and primary-part APIs are also unavailable on the projection. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

Character.Orientation is a write-only visual rotation channel in Vortex: assigning Vector3.new(0, 90, 0) visibly quarter-turns the character, yet reading it returns nil before and after the write. It differs from Player.Orientation, which retains an assigned value with no visible turn, and from HumanoidRootPart, which rejects the write. After a turn, Orientation, Rotation, and CFrame all remain nil on Player, Character, Humanoid, Scene, armature, limbs, and Head, so the resulting yaw cannot be read back. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

questions: What is Character visual Scene projection?
Explain Character visual Scene projection in Vortex
How do I use Character visual Scene projection?
Tell me about Character visual Scene projection
answer: Character:GetChildren() returns an unnamed generic Instance that, after a short loading delay, exposes a Scene property containing the rendered armature, body meshes, limbs, and avatar-specific attachments. Access it via character:GetChildren()[1].Scene, then bracket-syntax for dotted or spaced names such as armature["Armature.001"], visualRoot.HumanoidRootPart, torso["Right Leg"], and so on. This visual HumanoidRootPart is not the restricted public character.HumanoidRootPart Part projection, and the visual HumanoidRootPart and Torso discard Orientation writes without error. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

questions: What is Character visual Scene replacement?
Explain Character visual Scene replacement in Vortex
How do I use Character visual Scene replacement?
Tell me about Character visual Scene replacement
answer: The visual Scene can be replaced while the Character itself remains available, and replacement destroys the old visual instances. Stored references to limbs or accessories from a previous Scene cannot be reparented into the new one, so you must resolve the current visual Scene again each time you need it. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

questions: Explain Character lifecycle limitation in Vortex
How do I use Character lifecycle limitation?
Tell me about Character lifecycle limitation
answer: The standard Player.CharacterAdded signal is not exposed in the tested Vortex runtime; it remained nil in both Script and LocalScript over a 15-second observation window. Instead of waiting on that signal, you should poll Player.Character and the visual Scene route to detect when a Character or its visuals are ready. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/character.md

Debris is a Vortex service accessed via game:GetService("Debris") that lets you schedule instances for automatic removal after a delay without yielding the current thread. It is useful for objects like temporary parts or effects that lose their purpose after some time. Typical usage involves calling Debris:AddItem(instance, seconds) on an instance after it has been parented into the game hierarchy. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/debris.md

AddItem is a method on the Debris service with the signature Debris:AddItem(instance: Instance, lifetime: Number). It schedules the given instance to be removed (its Parent set to nil) after lifetime seconds, without yielding the calling thread. It is exposed in both Script and LocalScript contexts, and testing notes indicate that calling it with a lifetime of 0 on an unparented temporary Part removed it within two scheduler ticks. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/debris.md

SetMaxItems is a method on the Debris service with the signature Debris:SetMaxItems(maxItems: Number). It sets the maximum number of instances that the Debris service will track at one time. This provides a configurable cap on how many pending-removal items the service manages simultaneously. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/debris.md

questions: Explain Debris testing notes in Vortex
How do I use Debris testing notes?
Tell me about Debris testing notes
answer: The Debris service was revalidated in Vortex Studio 0.3.4, with the caveat that detailed behavior may differ in later releases. Both AddItem and SetMaxItems are available in Script and LocalScript contexts. In one test, calling Debris:AddItem(part, 0) on an unparented temporary Part caused it to be removed within two scheduler ticks, after which the held Lua reference returned ClassName as Instance and Name as an empty string. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/debris.md

Folder is a general-purpose container for instances in Vortex, available as a constructable type in both Script and LocalScript starting from Vortex Studio 0.3.4. It supports standard instance and hierarchy operations such as FindFirstChild, GetChildren, GetDescendants, and WaitForChild. However, Folders created at runtime have a significant limitation: they cannot form an observable hierarchy, meaning setting a Part's Parent to such a Folder does not make the child visible via Parent equality or hierarchy queries, and parenting the Folder itself to Workspace similarly fails to register it. The recommended practice is to author Folders in the editor for organization rather than trying to build folder hierarchies dynamically at runtime. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/folder.md

questions: What is Folder runtime hierarchy limitation?
Explain Folder runtime hierarchy limitation in Vortex
How do I use Folder runtime hierarchy limitation?
Tell me about Folder runtime hierarchy limitation
answer: In Vortex, a Folder instantiated by a script cannot establish a working runtime hierarchy. Reparenting objects under such a Folder causes child.Parent to still evaluate to nil, while FindFirstChild, GetChildren, GetDescendants, and WaitForChild all fail to surface those children. Similarly, parenting the runtime Folder to Workspace does not make it discoverable through Workspace lookups or GetChildren. To avoid these issues, developers should create Folders in the editor when organizing instances and avoid relying on script-created Folders for hierarchy purposes. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/folder.md

HumanoidRootPart is the root Part exposed by a visible player's Character Model in Vortex. Although its ClassName reports as "Part", it functions as a narrow character-state projection rather than a full Part instance and is not separately constructible. You access it through the Character of a Player, such as via Players.LocalPlayer.Character.HumanoidRootPart in a LocalScript, or via a server Script using Players:GetPlayers()[1].Character.HumanoidRootPart. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid-root-part.md

questions: Explain HumanoidRootPart Confirmed Surface in Vortex
How do I use HumanoidRootPart Confirmed Surface?
Tell me about HumanoidRootPart Confirmed Surface
answer: The confirmed surface lists properties and methods readable from HumanoidRootPart in Vortex Studio 0.3.4 from both LocalScript and server Script contexts. Readable fields include ClassName (value "Part"), Name (value "HumanoidRootPart"), Parent (the Character Model), Position (Vector3), and Size (Vector3). IsA is the only exposed method and returns true for "Part", "BasePart", and "Instance". Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid-root-part.md

questions: Explain HumanoidRootPart Unavailable Fields in Vortex
How do I use HumanoidRootPart Unavailable Fields?
Tell me about HumanoidRootPart Unavailable Fields
answer: Many standard Part and Instance fields and methods are unavailable on HumanoidRootPart and read as nil. Tested unavailable Part fields include Anchored, CanCollide, CastShadow, CFrame, Color, Material, Orientation, Rotation, Transparency, and various velocity, mass, collision-query, touch, and root-priority properties. Tested unavailable methods include hierarchy, clone, destroy, attributes, property signals, joints, impulses, mass, and network ownership methods, along with the Changed, Touched, and TouchEnded signals which are not connectable. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid-root-part.md

questions: Explain HumanoidRootPart Character-State Authority in Vortex
How do I use HumanoidRootPart Character-State Authority?
Tell me about HumanoidRootPart Character-State Authority
answer: Writing to HumanoidRootPart transform fields is rejected in both LocalScript and server Script contexts. Attempting to set Position, Size, or Orientation produces an error that calls the property read-only in a LocalScript and states character state is server-authoritative even when RunService:IsServer() returns true. As a result, the visible character root part should not be used as a server-side teleport, resize, or movement-control target, although ordinary script-created Parts remain writable. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid-root-part.md

Humanoid represents the humanoid controller attached to a Player Character in Vortex. In a LocalScript, the local player's Humanoid can be accessed via `game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer.Character.Humanoid`, while as of Vortex Studio 0.3.4 a server Script can also reach a visible player's character through `game:GetService("Players"):GetPlayers()[1].Character`. The character's root transform is exposed separately via the HumanoidRootPart. The Humanoid value is a specialized table exposing properties like Health and MaxHealth, the IsDead() method, and the Died and HealthChanged signals. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

ClassName is a String property on a Humanoid that reports the class name of the object. In observed cases it returns the literal value `"Humanoid"`. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

Name is a String property on a Humanoid that holds the Humanoid's name. In observed cases it also reports the value `"Humanoid"`. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

Health is a Number property on a Humanoid that holds the current health value, observed to report 100. Attempting to assign to it is rejected in both a LocalScript and a server Script, making it read-only from a client's perspective and not server-authoritative for writes in tested builds. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

MaxHealth is a Number property on a Humanoid that holds the maximum health value, observed to report 100. Like Health, assigning to MaxHealth is rejected from both LocalScript and server Script contexts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

IsDead is a method on a Humanoid called via `humanoid:IsDead()` that returns a Boolean. It reports whether the Humanoid is currently dead, and was observed to return `false` on a live character. It is the only confirmed method on the server-side Humanoid projection; Roblox-style methods like TakeDamage and movement/animator methods all read as nil. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

Died is a Signal exposed on a Humanoid via `humanoid.Died` that fires when the Humanoid dies. It is one of only two connectable signals on the tested Humanoid projection and supports `Signal:Connect`, although actual signal delivery in this build was unconfirmed. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

HealthChanged is a Signal exposed on a Humanoid via `humanoid.HealthChanged` that fires when the Humanoid's health value changes. Its callback receives a single Number parameter named `health` containing the updated health value, and it supports `Signal:Connect` though signal delivery was unconfirmed in testing. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

questions: Explain Humanoid server-script access in Vortex
How do I use Humanoid server-script access?
Tell me about Humanoid server-script access
answer: As of Vortex Studio 0.3.4, server Scripts can enumerate Players, read a player's Character, and obtain its Humanoid via `game:GetService("Players"):GetPlayers()[1].Character`. However, this server-visible Humanoid projection does not grant Health-write authority, and Roblox-style properties like WalkSpeed, JumpPower, JumpHeight, and UseJumpPower all read as nil on it, so their write behavior is unknown. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/humanoid.md

Instance is the base class from which all classes in the Vortex engine inherit. It defines a small common surface consisting of two properties, Name and Parent, along with three methods: Clone, Destroy, and GetChildren. Every object placed into the engine's object hierarchy is ultimately an Instance or a subclass of it. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

Name is a property of the Instance class of type String that holds the display name of the object. It can be read and assigned to identify the Instance within its hierarchy or in code. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

Parent is a property of the Instance class that is either another Instance or nil. It represents the object's position in the hierarchical tree; setting it to nil detaches the object, while assigning an Instance adopts it as a child of that parent. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

Clone is a method on the Instance class that takes no arguments and returns a new Instance. The returned object is a duplicate of the original, including its properties and descendants, and is created without a parent. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

Destroy is a method on the Instance class that removes the object and all of its descendants from the hierarchy, returning nil. Once called, the Instance and its children are no longer accessible through their previous Parent. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

GetChildren is a method on the Instance class that returns an array of Instance values, representing the direct children of the object. It does not recurse into those descendants; only the immediate children of the calling Instance are included in the returned table. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/instance.md

IntValue is an integer value container available in Vortex Studio 0.3.4, constructable from both Script and LocalScript contexts. Unlike many Vortex instances, it does not require a parent to read or write its stored number. It is a detached, lightweight object holding a single integral Value property. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/int-value.md

Name is a string property on IntValue representing the instance's display name. A newly constructed IntValue is given the default name "IntValue". This property is a string type and can be reassigned like any standard instance name. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/int-value.md

Value is a number property on IntValue that holds the stored integer. A freshly created IntValue starts at 0. The property supports both reading and assignment of integral numbers, as shown in typical usage such as setting a score to 42 and reading it back. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/int-value.md

questions: What is IntValue Changed signal behavior?
Explain IntValue Changed signal behavior in Vortex
How do I use IntValue Changed signal behavior?
Tell me about IntValue Changed signal behavior
answer: IntValue exposes the Changed event and GetPropertyChangedSignal("Value") method, and both can be connected to callbacks. However, in the tested 0.3.4 runtime, mutating Value did not actually invoke either signal. Code that needs to react to Value changes should poll the property instead of relying on change notifications. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/int-value.md

questions: Explain Instance.new for IntValue in Vortex
How do I use Instance.new for IntValue?
Tell me about Instance.new for IntValue
answer: Instance.new("IntValue") constructs a new IntValue instance in Vortex. The resulting object has Value defaulting to 0 and Name defaulting to "IntValue". It can be used immediately for reading and writing integral values without parenting it to an object hierarchy. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/int-value.md

Lighting is a built-in Vortex game service that governs basic rendering and atmospherics for a place. It cannot be created or destroyed by scripts. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, however, `game:GetService("Lighting")` fails because the service is not yet registered as a runtime service in either Script or LocalScript contexts, so the documented properties are only accessible through editor-facing controls. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

questions: How do I use Ambient Color?
answer: Ambient Color is a Lighting property of type Color3 that determines the visible color of ambient lighting. It also affects the color produced by a part's Material. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

Brightness is a Lighting property of type Float that controls how bright the ambient lighting is in the scene. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

questions: How do I use Sun Color?
answer: Sun Color is a Lighting property of type Color3 that determines the color of the sunlight hitting objects. It blends with the ambient coloring to produce the final lit appearance. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

questions: How do I use Sun Brightness?
answer: Sun Brightness is a Lighting property of type Float that determines how bright the directional sun light appears on surfaces. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

questions: How do I use Sun Shadows?
answer: Sun Shadows is a Lighting property of type Boolean that globally toggles shadows cast by the sun. Because no other light types produce shadows, it effectively acts as a global on/off switch for all shadowing in the game. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

Position is a Lighting property of type Vector3 that has no effect on rendering. It is listed under Lighting for completeness but does not influence lighting or atmospherics. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

Rotation is a Lighting property of type Vector3 that determines the angle at which sunlight strikes objects. Changing it shifts the direction of the sun and therefore the size and orientation of cast shadows. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

Size is a Lighting property of type Vector3 that is read-only and has no effect on rendering. It is exposed on Lighting but does not influence the scene. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/lighting.md

A LocalScript is a type of Luau script in Vortex that runs on the client side, meaning it executes on the player's local machine rather than on the server. It is intended for client-only behavior such as UI logic, camera control, and input handling, and should not be used for server-authoritative logic. LocalScripts have key properties including Parent (an Instance specifying where the script lives, such as a PlayerGui or StarterPlayerScripts), Disabled (a Boolean indicating whether the script is currently disabled), and Source (a String representing the script's code, which may be read-only in some tools and is not guaranteed at runtime). LocalScripts do not execute in server-only containers like ServerScriptService, and code that requires Players.LocalPlayer will only work inside a LocalScript since LocalPlayer is nil on the server. For security, client-side code should never be trusted for authoritative logic, permissions, or game state — that validation must happen on the server. Typical placements for LocalScripts include StarterPlayerScripts, StarterGui/PlayerGui, StarterCharacterScripts, and Backpack (for tool-local behavior). Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/localscript.md

In Vortex, a Model is an explorer-level grouping of Parts used purely for organization. Creating one requires selecting at least 2 parts, after which the second part may be deleted; the model has no physical connection between its children. An empty model still appears in the explorer but has no world presence and no transform handles. Move and Rotate tools work on models, but scaling is not properly supported. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

Model.Name is a String property that sets the model's display label in the explorer. It is the same as the standard Instance Name field and follows the usual naming rules. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

Model.Position is a Vector3 property representing the model's center in World-space. It is automatically computed as the mathematical average of all the model's child positions, so it is not independently settable in the normal sense. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: Explain Model Testing Notes in Vortex
How do I use Model Testing Notes?
Tell me about Model Testing Notes
answer: Testing Notes in Vortex 0.3.4 document that a detached Model only exposes the generic Instance surface, with no readable Position, PrimaryPart, or WorldPivot. Parenting a Part to a detached Model does not produce a real hierarchy: parent equality is false, FindFirstChild returns nil, GetChildren returns an empty table, and WaitForChild never returns the part. Pivot APIs (GetPivot, PivotTo, GetPrimaryPartCFrame, SetPrimaryPartCFrame) are nil, and assigning Model.PrimaryPart is rejected. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: How do I use Character Model?
answer: The live Character Model in Vortex 0.3.4 is a special case that exposes ClassName, Name, Position, plus direct Humanoid and HumanoidRootPart members, while Parent reads as nil. It supports the generic Instance method surface and a connectable Changed signal, but its tested hierarchy and lifecycle signals are unavailable. Like a detached Model, its pivot and primary-part APIs are not accessible. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: What is Character Write-only Visual Rotation?
Explain Character Write-only Visual Rotation in Vortex
How do I use Character Write-only Visual Rotation?
Tell me about Character Write-only Visual Rotation
answer: In Vortex 0.3.4, the live Character Model is a verified write-only visual rotation target. Assigning character.Orientation = Vector3.new(0, 90, 0) in a server Script visibly turns the character, but the field still reads back as nil. This is the only documented write that produces an observable visual change on the Character without a readable return value. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: Explain Character Visual Scene in Vortex
How do I use Character Visual Scene?
Tell me about Character Visual Scene
answer: After the visual character finishes loading, Character:GetChildren() returns one unnamed generic Instance that can expose a Scene member. This Scene is a separate, transient render hierarchy distinct from the public Character projection. Code that depends on it must poll and re-resolve it after every replacement, since it can change at runtime. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: Explain Character Armature Path in Vortex
How do I use Character Armature Path?
Tell me about Character Armature Path
answer: Once the transient Character Scene resolves, its primary rig is indexable as scene['Armature.001'], which contains HumanoidRootPart, Torso, Head, and limb children such as 'Left Arm' and 'Right Leg'. Bracket indexing is required for names containing dots like 'Armature.001' and for limb names containing spaces. This inner rig is separate from the public Character.HumanoidRootPart Part projection. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: Explain Visual Rig Properties in Vortex
How do I use Visual Rig Properties?
Tell me about Visual Rig Properties
answer: Visual rig and attachment nodes in Vortex report ClassName == 'Instance' and expose the generic hierarchy and attribute methods, plus readable Name, Parent, Position, and Size. Changed, Touched, and TouchEnded can be connected, but no delivery was observed when a limb's Position updated, so the values are readable render state rather than a substitute for the public HumanoidRootPart projection. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

questions: Explain Visual Rig Transparency in Vortex
How do I use Visual Rig Transparency?
Tell me about Visual Rig Transparency
answer: Visual rig and attachment nodes in Vortex accept numeric Transparency writes from both LocalScripts and server Scripts. An initially unset value reads as nil, but after writing 0.5 or 0 it reads back as that numeric value. The tested torso and leg did not visibly change, so this is currently stored projection state rather than a confirmed render-opacity control, unlike the public HumanoidRootPart which rejects the same write. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/model.md

ModuleScript is a class in Vortex that represents a non-executable runtime module shell. It can be instantiated in both Script and LocalScript contexts starting with Vortex Studio 0.3.4, but it cannot be turned into a functioning module at runtime. Assigning one to ReplicatedStorage does not establish an observable parent-child relationship. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: Explain ModuleScript runtime construction in Vortex
How do I use ModuleScript runtime construction?
Tell me about ModuleScript runtime construction
answer: In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, a ModuleScript can be created at runtime from within Script or LocalScript contexts, but it is not a usable module. The properties Source, Disabled, and RunContext all read as nil when accessed on such a runtime instance, and any attempt to assign Source is rejected. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: Explain ModuleScript Source property in Vortex
How do I use ModuleScript Source property?
Tell me about ModuleScript Source property
answer: Source is a property of ModuleScript that holds the module's code. On a ModuleScript constructed at runtime in Vortex, reading Source returns nil, and writing to Source is not allowed, so the shell cannot be supplied with executable code. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: Explain ModuleScript Disabled property in Vortex
How do I use ModuleScript Disabled property?
Tell me about ModuleScript Disabled property
answer: Disabled is a property of ModuleScript that normally controls whether the module runs. On a runtime-instantiated ModuleScript in Vortex, reading Disabled yields nil rather than a boolean value. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: Explain ModuleScript RunContext property in Vortex
How do I use ModuleScript RunContext property?
Tell me about ModuleScript RunContext property
answer: RunContext is a property of ModuleScript indicating the execution context in which the module runs. When a ModuleScript is created at runtime in Vortex, reading RunContext returns nil, since the instance cannot be promoted to a real module. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: Explain require and ModuleScript in Vortex
How do I use require and ModuleScript?
Tell me about require and ModuleScript
answer: The global require function is not available in Vortex's runtime environment. Because require is unavailable, a ModuleScript that was constructed at runtime cannot deliver shared executable code to other scripts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

questions: What is ModuleScript and ReplicatedStorage parenting?
Explain ModuleScript and ReplicatedStorage parenting in Vortex
How do I use ModuleScript and ReplicatedStorage parenting?
Tell me about ModuleScript and ReplicatedStorage parenting
answer: Assigning a runtime-created ModuleScript to ReplicatedStorage in Vortex does not produce an observable child-parent relationship. The instance is effectively a non-functional shell and is not surfaced as a child of the destination container. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/modulescript.md

Player is an instance that represents a connected client in Vortex. The current client is exposed through the Players service as Players.LocalPlayer, accessible from a LocalScript. In Vortex Studio 0.3.4, the Player surface only reliably exposes the fields ClassName (the string "Player"), Name, and Character. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.Name is a property holding the player's display name. It is one of the three non-nil fields (along with ClassName and Character) observed on a Player in both server Scripts and LocalScripts during the 0.3.4 surface probe. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.ClassName is a string property that reads as "Player" for the current client projection. It is exposed as a non-nil field on Player instances in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.Character is a property that references the player's current Character Model when one is available. In the observed runtime projection, the Character contains a Humanoid and a HumanoidRootPart, both of which are direct readable members rather than results returned from Player:GetChildren(). Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.Position begins as nil but accepts and retains an assigned Vector3 value in both server Scripts and LocalScripts. However, it does not update the public Character.HumanoidRootPart and the values are context-local, so a server-side write is not visible to a client observer and vice versa. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.Rotation starts as nil and is writable, accepting CFrame rotation values in both server and client contexts. It does not translate into motion of the Character's HumanoidRootPart and the retained values are isolated per writer, so it should not be used as a movement or replication channel. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.CFrame is initially nil and behaves like the Position and Rotation projection fields: it accepts an assigned CFrame but does not move the visible Character. It is one of the writable but context-local Player fields tested in Vortex Studio 0.3.4. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Player.Orientation is a writable Vector3 projection field that begins as nil and retains assigned values. It is not a verified route for visually rotating the Character; Character.Orientation should be used instead when the goal is to turn the rendered character. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

questions: What are Player transform projection fields?
Explain Player transform projection fields in Vortex
How do I use Player transform projection fields?
Tell me about Player transform projection fields
answer: Player transform projection fields are Position, CFrame, and Rotation, which start as nil but accept assigned Vector3/CFrame values in both server and client contexts. They do not affect the public Character's HumanoidRootPart and the written values are kept separately by each context, making them unreliable for character movement, replicated state, or a server-client metadata channel. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Players.LocalPlayer returns the Player instance representing the current client and is available inside a LocalScript. It is nil inside a normal server Script, and its Parent reads as nil. Server scripts can instead obtain Players through Players:GetPlayers(). Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/player.md

Players is a service in Vortex that represents all clients currently connected to the game as Player objects. It can be accessed via game:GetService("Players") and is commonly used in both LocalScripts and server Scripts. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

GetPlayers() is a method on the Players service that returns an array of currently visible Player objects. In a LocalScript it returns the player list as seen by that client, and in a server Script it returns a list containing the live Player object whose Character can be read. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

LocalPlayer is a property on the Players service that returns the local Player object for the current client. It is only available in a LocalScript; on the server it is nil. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

Name is a property on the Players service that holds the name of the service, typically "Players". Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

ClassName is a property on the Players service that returns the runtime class name of the object, such as "Players". Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

questions: What are the Players service limitations?
Explain Players service limitations in Vortex
How do I handle Players service limitations?
Tell me about Players service limitations
answer: The Players service in Vortex does not expose GetChildren for enumerating its children, and there is no known public mapping from the numeric connection id passed as the first OnServerEvent argument back to a specific Player. Numeric or string indexing of services and tested player lookup methods do not provide that connection id to Player mapping. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/players.md

PointLight is a class in Vortex that represents a spherical light emitting from a single point. It must be parented to a Part, and it inherits its world position from that parent Part. There is no on/off toggle, but you can simulate turning the light off by setting its Color, Brightness, or Range to 0. Source: https://github.com/TheHaloDeveloper/vortex-docs/blob/main/content/reference/classes/point-light.md
